To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the functional organization of the neuronal network controlling behavior in terrestrial snails is modular, and that the network controlling behavior in snail is organized in the form of 'hard-wired','soft-wired', and 'hard-and-soft-wired' modules.

the behavioral plasticity in gastropod snails is mediated by two distinct mechanisms: a) the long-term changes in synaptic strength in identified neurons, and b) the long-term effects on the behavior produced by a single modulatory (reinforcement) neuron.
In summary, our research is concerned with
cellular mechanisms of learning and memory, and the principles of their organization.
the mechanisms of behavioral plastic in a model system, which allows to study cellular and molecular mechanisms of learning and memory in the simplest possible way.
the functional organization of the central nervous system in the terrestrial snail Helix and its changes during behavioral modifications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanisms of behavioral plasticities are not universal but depend on the functional organization of the network and on the type of behavior.
the principles of plasticity are different in different functional classes of networks.
behavioral plasticity in gastropod snails is a result of a complex interplay of different types of synaptic and non-synaptic mechanisms, which are mediated by different classes of identified neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the functional organization of the Helix nervous system is a model for the general principles of the nervous system organization.
plasticity of neuronal networks is based on the combination of hard-wired changes in synaptic connectivity and soft-wired neuromodulatory mechanisms.
the behavioral plasticity in snails is a result of the interaction between the hard-wired and soft-wired components of the neural networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the principles of behavioral plasticity are similar in different species of terrestrial gastropod mollusks, including humans.
a simple nervous system of the snail can be used to study the mechanisms of learning and memory, which are evolutionarily conserved in higher animals.

the principles formulated on the basis of the data from the terrestrial snail can be extended to other model systems and can be useful in the analysis of plasticity at different levels of organization.
